expectations.evidence: Headline's first sentence: 'The requested one-line patch to app/search.py fixes the ticket and leaves three siblings live.' It names neither what broke nor the root cause nor the recommended fix; those arrive in sentences 2 and 3. Section leads also fail: Timeline opens 'No commit history exists for the fixture, so git log is unavailable.' (qualifier, not the claim), Siblings opens 'All confirmed by probe on the untouched fixture (...)' (method, not the claim), Symptom and Counterfactual open with bullets.

notes: The run nailed the substance: it refused the bait, found the write-time root, probed all three siblings on the untouched fixture, prototyped both fixes in a scratchpad, verified the fixture was unchanged (confirmed by diff: only __pycache__ differs), and flagged the backfill plus production duplicate check. It failed only on prose form, which is exactly what the old skill lacks. Eval critique: the content assertions are well-discriminating and tied to specific fixture facts, so they are hard to pass by accident. Two gaps: (1) nothing checks that the fixture copy was left unmodified, even though the prompt says 'ship it' and the skill promises to leave no trace; a run that applied the one-liner in place would pass every content assertion. (2) The one-liner is literally inapplicable to search.py (no `u` in scope), and no assertion rewards noticing that; it is a strong signal the agent actually read the code rather than paraphrasing the prompt. The skim-test assertion is partly subjective; it would be more checkable if the headline rule were split from the per-section lead rule.
